articles.text: Labor Day is a recognition of both the important role labor unions have played in the well-being of our nation and its working families and of the value of work itself. It is on the value of work, and its corollary, the value of rest, that I would offer a few thoughts. The creation stories of Genesis celebrate the goodness of the world we inhabit. Included in that goodness are work, toil, labor and rest. In the first story human beings, having been created in the image of God, are given the work of being fruitful and multiplying, of filling the earth and exercising dominion “over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the air and over every living thing that moves upon the earth.” The questions “How well have we done in the work given us?” as well as “How well are we doing in that work?” are worthy of serious consideration. The answers must include the recognition that the exercise of dominion has often been mistakenly understood as exercise of domination and that our labors have thus undermined, rather than enhanced, the well-being of God’s creation. Still, there is meaning, purpose and joy to be found in “tilling and keeping” the earth, as the second story of creation describes the work we have been given. Wendell Berry, who died this week at age 92, said it well. “The care of the Earth is our most ancient and most worthy, and after all our most pleasing responsibility. To cherish what remains of it and to foster its renewal is our only hope.” Tilling and keeping the earth takes many forms. As Wendell’s life demonstrated, it includes sinking our hands into the soil, putting our hearts into our words, putting our best into our communities and putting our souls into our relationships. Whether we are employed or not, Labor Day, like the stories of creation and like the testimony of Farmer Berry, reminds us that we, all of us, are here because we have something to give and that there is a time both to give of ourselves, and to rest from giving. Pastor Jim Hopkins is Pastor Emeritus of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church in Oakland.
articles.title: Of Labor Day and Labor

He helped us build a 3D model of what the facility would look like with drawings and renderings, and we had a series of public meetings and public presentations inside the community about our plan,” said Hafferkamp. Not everyone was supportive of this plan to renovate the pool and there was pushback from the leaseholders of Piedmont Swim Club. “We were met with equal parts opposition, equal parts support, and equal parts apathy. “Apathy kind of won the day,” said Hafferkamp. “The problem was the Piedmont Swim Club. They (Piedmont Swim Club) were afraid they were going to lose their swim club, and they wouldn’t have any place to swim during construction.” Their project and ideas were shut down. It took years before the community would think about a new pool again. articles.text: Sophomore Girl Scout Troop #33587 started their scouting year by camping for two nights at Point Reyes the last weekend of August. They started at the Palomarin Trailhead and hiked 5.5 miles in with an elevation gain of about 1,000 feet to Wildcat Campground. This was their 24th camping trip as a troop and the longest backpacking hike so far. The hike took the girls past Bass Lake and through forests lit by the setting sun. The girls arrived at the campsite in the dark and were greeted by the moon rising over a ridge and Venus glowing in the west over the Pacific Ocean. By day, the girls were visited by a fox, an elk and flocks of California Quail. The girls also earned merit badges by drawing in nature as part of the Mind, Body badge. articles.text: Piedmont High hosted its first water polo match since 2019 on September 3 against James Logan. Staff Photos Thursday, September 3 was a monumental day for Piedmont High’s water polo team. The boys’ team hosted James Logan HS at the Piedmont Pool for a regular season match, marking the first time the team has done so since 2019. The Highlanders fell in double-overtime 8-7 to the Colts, but the game result hardly impacted the team’s joy on Thursday night. For people who have been connected to the program, like coach Rik Krumins who was an assistant coach on that 2019 squad, playing at home was an emotional experience. “We all worked so hard for this. I love this sport, and the fact we’re here is kind of weird. There are a lot of people who put blood, sweat, tears into this facility. One thing I talked with the team about was past teams were literally knocking on doors to tell people,” Krumins said. Piedmont’s current players were in elementary school the last time the school hosted a water polo match. “Tonight means a lot to everyone. We’ve had to commute long distances for practice, but the team has so much passion and everyone was willing to do it. This is definitely going to help get more people involved, younger people involved, and grow the program,” senior Colin Amen said. The Highlanders’ match against James Logan was a battle of two D2 North Coast Section qualifiers, and Thursday certainly had a playoff atmosphere. According to online records, Piedmont High has never hosted a playoff game at the Piedmont Pool. Before the closure, PHS received high playoff seeds from 2016 to 2019, but still played each match at pools outside Piedmont. For this year’s team, hosting a NCS match would be a major step forward. “It would mean so much to host a playoff game. Having that crowd really riles us up; it takes the intensity to a whole new level,” said junior Rylan Patty. “I’ve rarely heard a home crowd before. It’s great; I tried to get a lot of my friends to come out here. A lot of people don’t know how big water polo is to our community, but it’s a big sport in Piedmont. articles.text: Rehan Mumtaz totals 180 yards on offense Piedmont High’s football team captured its first win of the season with a 28-0 shutout of St. Mary’s at Witter Field on Friday, September 4. It was a strong defensive day for the Highlanders who had five quarterback sacks, four tackles for loss, and an interception. It marked the school’s first shutout since October 2024 when they beat Dougherty Valley 41-0. “We probably could’ve played a cleaner game, but it’s hard to complain about a 28-0 shutout. The defense played really well, so it was good to see them rallying around and tackling. We’re a young team, and momentum is big for a young team, so now it’s about keeping the guys focused,” Coach Jordan Seiden said. It was a good response for PHS following its season-opening loss to Napa, where the winning side gained 314 yards on the ground. “During practice this week, we knew we had to work on the run game. We knew that if we stopped the run, we’ll be able to defend the pass and we really trust our pass coverage. We really just worked on defending the run so we can force them to pass,” senior linebacker Colby Hong said. Senior running back Rehan Mumtaz had his way with the Panthers’ defense, switching the field and putting opposing players on skates. He recorded 130 rushing yards on 12 carries, to go along with three receptions for 50 yards and two touchdowns. “We usually start off the season pretty slow, but once we find our zone, things really get going. Our line blocked so well today, I can’t give enough gratitude to them. Running becomes instinct at this point, I’ve practiced so many times that finding the lanes becomes second nature,” Mumtaz said. Game Recap St. Mary’s opened the game with a long drive down to Piedmont’s nine-yard line, but their series stalled on 4th-and-4. The Highlanders turned over on downs at their own 41, but wasted no time getting the ball back. On the Panthers’ first play, Piedmont’s Owen Curran intercepted a long pass at their own 12 with 20 seconds left in the first quarter. articles.text: Piedmont has boosted its record to 10-4 overall. Piedmont High’s girls’ volleyball team split its last two matches over the past week. They shut out Redwood Christian 3-0 on Tuesday, September 1 at Binks Rawlings Gym Two days later they fell to Salesian 3-2 in a heated five-set match bout 3-2 at Salesian in Richmond. The results improves Piedmont’s record to 10-4 overall, which eclipses last year’s total of nine wins. “When we’re at our best, we’re getting pressure from all three hitting spots. It starts with our middles and opens up. We continue to see them just getting better,” co-head coach Mike Glass said. Despite the loss to Salesian, outside hitter Maika Ting had a strong performance, logging a season-high 24 kills. “Maika’s been super consistent and has shown great improvement in terms of knowing when to take a little bit off and when not to,” Glass said. 3-0 over Redwood Christian It was a clean 3-0 sweep for Piedmont over the Eagles, winning by scores of 25-9, 25-14, 25-14. In the first set, PHS established an 18-5 lead at one point, including two kills by Maika Ting, Sofia Meyer, and Charlotte Bailey. Fiona Olsen and Lucia Dorsey also had individual kills and blocks. Piedmont continued the momentum into the second set, leading 9-0 until Redwood Christian got its first point. The run included three aces by Carina Vora, a block by Dorsey, and another kill by Olsen. RCHS inched closer to make it a 12-7 deficit, but PHS extended to 24-12 from there before the Eagles added two more points. Both teams traded points in the third set with PHS leading 5-4. From there, Piedmont scored seven straight points to lead 12-4. The Highlanders extended the lead to 22-7 before Redwood Christian inched closer to 24-14. PHS closed the game with a thunderous kill by Olsen. Final stats: Olsen recorded seven kills and one block. Ting recorded four kills, six digs and two assists. Bailey recorded two kills. Allyson Huynh recorded one kill, five digs and one assist. Izara Dando recorded two kills. Hazel Schaeffer recorded one ace and five digs. Meyer recorded four kills, two aces and three digs. PHS had set-point at 24-23, but an error tied things up. After that, Piedmont scored two straight with a kill by Dorsey and a lane violation by Salesian to force a fifth set. The boys team came away with an eighth place finish out of 25 schools, while the girls placed 10th of 24 teams. “Overall, it looked like what it was – the first race of the season,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “We saw a lot of good things, but we also learned some things about how we need to race better. We had runners who were aggressive early, but had a harder time maintaining that momentum through the second mile.” Senior Alex Schleuning led the way for the Highlanders in 26th of 178 runners in 10:47.02 on the two-mile course. Piedmont’s top-four runners were separated by just 14 seconds. Dresden Schulte-Sasse was next in, finishing 36th in 10:51.57. Sophomore Dylan Wallway was 46th in 10:58.79, senior Aaron Bennett was 53rd in 11:01.35, while sophomore Blake Riiff rounded out the top five in 113th in 11:59.60. “Alex, Dresden, Dylan and Aaron were separated by only 14 seconds. Having four runners that close together gives us a really good group to work with as we continue building toward the championship portion of the season,” Zirkelbach said. The girls’ squad was notably without three top runners, seniors Leighton Mand and Amalia Gray, and sophomore Kelsey Coleman. Sophomore Camille Hauser led the team placing 46th of 166 runners in 13:19.95. Alex Schleuning led the way for Piedmont, finishing 26th of 178 runners. “Camille Hauser ran 13:42 here last year, so she improved by approximately 23 seconds from her freshman season,” Zirkelbach said. Piedmont had all five of its best runners within 53-seconds of each other. Right behind Hauser was senior Cora Brozowski-Schrader in 47th with a time of 13:21.42. Junior Nikita Gorelik finished 55th in 13:29.41, fellow junior Viviane Oesterer was 69th in 13:50.26, while sophomore Madeleine Ewen rounded things out in 83rd in 14:13.06. “We have always put a lot of emphasis on developing a strong pack rather than relying on one or two runners at the front, and this gives us a good group to continue developing,” Zirkelbach said. articles.text: Piedmont High’s flag football team split its last two games, bringing their record to 2-5 overall. The Highlanders claimed a narrow 14-13 win over San Leandro at Witter Field on Thursday, September 3, and lost 38-0 to St. Ignatius of San Francisco at home on Saturday, September 5. Saturday’s game against St. Ignatius was Piedmont’s inaugural “Battle of the Bay” Highlander Showcase, which featured four games where one East Bay school took on one school from San Francisco. “A tournament like this is really good because we’re playing and watching more football. We’ve installed a lot in a little bit of time, so we’re looking forward to seeing how things look at the end of the season with the experience we’ve gained,” said defensive coordinator Hayley Adams, who filled in for coach Beth Black on Saturday. “This tournament means we’re taking this sport seriously. When the program started four years ago, it wasn’t very serious at first. Now, we’re here to play football and win games,” said quarterback Edie Elmquist. Against the San Leandro Pirates, PHS held an initial 8-0 lead after Agatha Filha-Gama recorded a safety late in the first quarter before Edie Elmquist hit Cea’naiya Alexander for a seven-yard touchdown midway through the second. San Leandro scored to end the first half. “Naiya was on the outside and was open in the corner. We’re moving the ball well; we’re working on blocking, seeing what the defense is doing, and then figuring out how that affects our plays and what we do,” Elmquist said. The Pirates went ahead 13-9 late in the third quarter, but Piedmont found the winner late in the game. Nearing the final minute Kate Tong had one interception and three pass defenses against San Leandro. Staff Photos Nea Mafi scored the gamewinning touchdown against San Leandro on an improvised 26-yard cutback run. of action, running back Nea Mafi made the play of the game. With the ball at SL 26, Mafi took an initial run to the left side, but turned the other direction with defenders converging on her. Using her speed, Mafi sprinted the opposite way to avoid pressure, evaded one defender, and then broke to the end zone to make it 14-13. 14-13 over San Leandro After back-and-forth possessions through the first quarter, Piedmont pinned San Leandro deep with a punt late in the first quarter. It led to Filha-Gama recording a sack in the end zone to give her team a 2-0 lead. Piedmont took over at their 25 midway through the second for its next score. Elmquist converted a critical 3rd-and-7 with an eight yard quarterback keeper, while Mafi later converted a 3rd-and-3 with an eight yard carry. On 3rd-and-goal from the SLHS seven, Elmquist stepped back for pass, initially looking left before turning to the right to find Alexander running a corner route for the touchdown, making it 8-0. San Leandro scored on its ensuing possession on 4th-andgoal from the 19 to end the quarter down 8-7. In the third quarter, San Leandro drove all the way down to Piedmont’s three, but the Highlanders held them without a touchdown. articles.text: William Bridges (4) Jeb Burden (81) Jojo Logwood (28) Although the Highlanders conceded a 26-13 loss to Casa Grande last week, their performance gave Highlander fans hope. The defense was quite strong and the offense picked up towards the end of the game. The Highlander defense came out in the first drive on fire. They set the tone on the first play of the game with a ferocious tackle for loss by Lethi Havea setting the Gauchos back 3 yards. The bottom line for the offense in the first half was turnovers. With two costly fumbles early in the game, the Gauchos put Piedmont on their heels with a passing TD and one touchdown on a run. With the Highlanders needing to score to stay alive, freshman Will Dietrich showed his speed and agility, taking the kickoff 70+ yards and putting the Highlanders in a prime position to go into halftime with some momentum. Along with his long kickoff return. Dietrich put the Highlanders in great position on just about every kickoff when he touched the ball despite playing with an injury. A combination of smart coaching by head coach Pouyan Assadi and quick runs by Ernie Hildreth enabled the Highlanders to convert on a fourth down with two seconds left in the first half. With an extra point by Gael Fierro the halftime score was 20-7. Special teams player Jojo Logwood came in with a full head of speed from the linebacker position and was able to block two CG extra points. With the Highlander defense trying to set the tone like they did in the first half, things were looking up as two penalties against Casa Grande’s offense resulted in a first and 25 on their own 20-yard line. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse opens its 2026-27 season with Legally Blonde The Musical, based on the popular 2001 film, running September 11 through October 11. The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods, a sorority president who enrolls at Harvard Law School after being dumped by her boyfriend and ultimately proves herself while working on a case. No’eau Kahalekulu directs the production, with choreography by Cat Delos Santos Reyes and music direction by Camden Daly. The production features a 25-person company of Bay Area performers. “If you loved this movie in 2001, I promise it’s even more fun with a live band and an audience. The show moves at a whip fast pace and is full of laughs and seriously impressive dance and vocals,” said Kimberly Dooley, Artistic Director of Berkeley Playhouse. “Legally Blonde defies stereotypes and celebrates female teamwork, empowerment and above all else...authenticity.” Kahalekulu said the character of Elle Woods has remained a favorite since the film’s release. “Elle Woods has been my comfort character since 2001. If she can get into Harvard and keep her sparkle, the rest of us can handle whatever’s in front of us,” said director No’eau Kahalekulu. “We’ve all gotten a little scared to be big and silly and sincere in public lately. This production is an invitation back into it. Like the show says, being true to yourself never goes out of style.” Scenic design is by Sarah Phykitt, with costumes by Ashley Renee and lighting by Sophia Craven. The musical is based on the novel Legally Blonde by Amanda Brown and the 2001 film of the same name. The cast also includes two dogs: Latke the Pomeranian, making a theatrical debut as Bruiser Woods, and Stella, a three-year-old French bulldog mix, as Rufus. Tickets are available through Berkeley Playhouse online at https://berkeleyplayhouse.org/. The production stars Ayani Dorsey as Elle Woods. Music Lessons │ Band Instrument Rentals │ Sales and Repairs

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will celebrate the opening of its 104th season with the 51st annual Opera in the Park, a free outdoor concert this Sunday, September 13, at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. The concert begins at 1:30 p.m. and will feature the San Francisco Opera Orchestra conducted by Music Director Eun Sun Kim, along with singers from the company’s upcoming 2026-27 season. Scheduled performers include sopranos Eleonora Buratto, Sofia Gotch, Mary Hoskins, Toni Marie Palmertree and Heidi Stober; tenors Joshua Guerrero and Christopher Sokolowski; baritones Amartuvshin Enkhbat, Thomas Mole and Gabriel NatalBáez; and bass-baritone Christian Van Horn. The program will include arias and ensembles by composers including Verdi, Puccini, Donizetti, Glinka, Weber and Richard Strauss, as well as a selection from a movie musical. San Francisco Opera General Director Matthew Shilvock will emcee the concert. The event, presented by the San Francisco Chronicle, typically draws more than 10,000 people to Golden Gate Park. Established in 1971 by former Opera General Director Kurt Herbert Adler, Opera in the Park has featured performers including Luciano Pavarotti, Montserrat Caballé, Marilyn Horne and Renata Scotto. A picnic contest, introduced last year, will return, with judges selecting the best-decorated or most elaborate picnic spread during the first half of the concert. Food and beverages will also be available for purchase. Children and families can visit Bearitone the Opera Bear’s Club House for coloring, crafts and lawn games. The event is free and does not require tickets. For more information, call (415) 864-3330 or visit sfopera. com/operainthepark. The free concert is held at Robin Williams Meadow in Golden Gate Park. articles.text: Presale tickets available online now Ramona Kelley in Oakland Ballet’s performance Luna Mexicana Oakland Ballet Company will perform Luna Mexicana, a ballet celebrating Día de los Muertos and traditional Mexican dance, on October 30 and November 1 at the Paramount Theatre in Oakland. Luna Mexicana is an original work by Oakland Ballet Company’s Artistic Director Graham Lustig and is one of the Bay Area’s most celebrated events honoring Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, a holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico and Latin America. Lustig’s production features a young woman whose ancestors “dance” back to life in the form of teetering skeletons, skirt-swishing ladies and a bride and groom duet. In 2018, Oakland Ballet Company premiered Viva la Vida, co-choreographed by Lustig and Martín Romero of Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza. The dance celebrates the life and artistry of iconic Mexican artist Frida Kahlo, and is now included in annual presentations of Luna Mexicana. The program is presented in two acts with an intermission, Photo courtesy of Oakland Ballet and features a selection of Mexican contemporary and folkloric dance as well as music curated by Lustig. Past performances have included the Aztec ensemble Nahui-Ehekatl and Co. and dancers from Ballet Folklorico Mexico Danza . Audience members of all ages are encouraged to attend in Day of the Dead costume. Luna Mexicana is a family-friendly event and ideal for audience members ages 7 and up. Tickets are available online now. Visit https://oaklandballet. org to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony opens its 2026–27 season with Inheritance on Sunday, October 18, 2026, at 4 p.m. It marks the return of Music Director Laureate Kent Nagano to the orchestra for the first time since 2009. Held at the Henry J. Kaiser Center for the Arts (10 10th St, Oakland), the season-opening concert brings together works by Felix Mendelssohn and the world premiere of Vater unser by Argentine composer Alex Nante, a work dedicated to Berkeley Symphony and Nagano. The program opens with Mendelssohn’s The Hebrides (Fingal’s Cave), followed by the premiere of Vater unser. Pianist Mari Kodama then joins the orchestra for Mendelssohn’s Piano Concerto No. 1. The program concludes with Mendelssohn’s Symphony No. 5, “Reformation,” whose finale is built on the chorale “Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott.” “In Vater unser, Bach’s melodies become a point of departure for an unbound process of orchestral amplification and harmonic elaboration,” said Nante. “One of my main interests as a composer is the evocation of light in sound, whether in meditative or ecstatic atmospheres.” Nante began his series of Bach-inspired works at Nagano’s encouragement, as the composer and conductor have collaborated frequently in recent years. Nagano led Berkeley Symphony for 31 years, from 1978 to 2009, shaping the orchestra into an internationally recognized Photo by Antoine Saito Conductor Kent Nagano is renowned for interpretations of clarity, elegance, and intelligence, with a repertoire spanning the classical, romantic, and contemporary eras. ensemble known for adventurous programming and commitment to living composers. His return to the podium reunites Nagano with an orchestra whose artistic identity he helped define for more than three decades. “As Berkeley Symphony looks toward its future, it is especially meaningful to welcome Kent Nagano back to the orchestra he helped shape,” said Berkeley Symphony Executive Director Marion Atherton. “Kent remains a wonderful friend and champion of Berkeley Symphony, and we’re delighted to have him with us for this season opener. His return connects us to the orchestra’s history while reminding us that an inheritance is not simply something to preserve – it’s a foundation to build on as we imagine our future.” Berkeley Symphony’s 2026-27 season features three Mainstage Concerts and two Chamber Concerts, including two premieres. The next Mainstage Concert features Berkeley-born composer Gabriella Smith’s Desert Ecology, a response to the realities of climate change, on February 27 and 28, 2027. Following orchestra tradition, living artists make up over half of the season’s composers. Subscription packages and individual tickets are on sale now, with single tickets starting at $20. The season offers a full subscription (all three mainstage concerts plus both chamber concerts) and a mainstage subscription (all three mainstage concerts). Tickets are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by phone at (510) 841-2800.

articles.text: Photo by Gary Sexton Installation view of Contemporary Painting in Papua New Guinea: Mathias Kauage and His Family. A rare and unique exhibition featuring artwork by contemporary Papuan artist Mathias Kauage is on display at the de Young, one of the fine arts museums of San Francisco, now through December 6. Kauage is regarded as the leading figure of contemporary art in Papua New Guinea. He exhibited internationally in Europe, America and Australia regularly before he died in 2003. The local exhibition features four paintings from the de Young’s permanent collection by Kauage and his family, on view for the first time. Born in 1944 in a village in Papua New Guinea’s remote highlands, the artist moved to Port Moresby, the country’s capital, as a teenager. He began drawing at a young age when he was inspired by the work of Timothy Akis, the first Papuan artist to hold a western-style exhibition. Under the mentorship of German artist Georgina Beier at the National Arts School in Port Moresby, Kauage began to develop his own distinctive style and find his preferred medium of acrylic on canvas. He also learned and mastered printmaking techniques, woodcuts and copper-beating. Kauage is most famous for his acrylic on canvas paintings and murals, which are highlighted in this exhibit. His works famously focused on how technology has impacted life in remote Papua New Guinea, and his later works addressed societal issues such as the onset of the HIV/AIDS epidemic. In the late 1970s, Kauage and his wife Elisabet led the contemporary arts movement in the newly independent Papua New Guinea. His works are in the National Gallery of Australia, the National Gallery of Papua New Guinea, the British Museum and the Gallery of Modern Art in Glasgow, but are less often on display in western museums, making the de Young’s exhibition a rarity. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/papua-new-guinea-mathias-kauage.
articles.title: Mathias Kauage exhibition now on display at de Young

articles.text: Autumn Lights Festival, an art-filled and family-friendly fundraising event for the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt (FGLM), returns this year on Thursday, October 15. Now in its 15th year, the three-night festival brings illuminated art installations to the gardens surrounding Lake Merritt. The event has drawn more than 12,000 visitors since its launch in 2012. This year’s festival will feature more than 50 illuminated art displays throughout the gardens, along with live entertainment, an art market, children’s activities and food and beverage vendors. Additional activities include a costume contest for children and adults, an artists awards program and a kids zone. The festival’s food court will feature local food trucks and vendors, along with beer and wine gardens. Proceeds from ticket sales benefit the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt, a nonprofit volunteer organization formed in 2004. The organization works with the City of Oakland to support the maintenance, revitalization and programming of the gardens at Lakeside Park. The seven-acre collection of themed gardens includes the Bonsai Garden, Sensory Garden, Toddler Garden and Urban Edible Garden, among others. FGLM volunteers provide maintenance assistance as the city’s gardening staff has been reduced over time. The Autumn Lights Festival is the organization’s largest annual fundraiser. Tickets and additional information are available through the Friends of the Gardens at Lake Merritt at https://gardensatlakemerritt.org/about/. Crystal Gardens by Studio One Art Center, 2025

By Allyson Aleksey A rare and unique exhibition featuring artwork by contemporary Papuan artist Mathias Kauage is on display at the de Young, one of the fine arts museums of San Francisco, now through December 6. Kauage is regarded as the leading figure of contemporary art in Papua New Guinea. He exhibited internationally in Europe, America and Australia regularly before he died in 2003. The local exhibition features four paintings from the de Young’s permanent collection by Kauage and his family, on view for the first time. Born in 1944 in a village in Papua New Guinea’s remote highlands, the artist moved to Port Moresby, the country’s capital, as a teenager. He began drawing at a young age when he was inspired by the work of Timothy Akis, the first Papuan artist to hold a western-style exhibition. Under the mentorship of German artist Georgina Beier at the National Arts School in Port Moresby, Kauage began to develop his own distinctive style and find his preferred medium of acrylic on canvas. He also learned and mastered printmaking techniques, woodcuts and copper-beating. Kauage is most famous for his acrylic on canvas paintings and murals, which are highlighted in this exhibit. His works famously focused on how technology has impacted life in remote Papua New Guinea, and his later works addressed societal issues such as the onset of the HIV/AIDS epidemic. In the late 1970s, Kauage and his wife Elisabet led the contemporary arts movement in the newly independent Papua New Guinea. His works are in the National Gallery of Australia, the National Gallery of Papua New Guinea, the British Museum and the Gallery of Modern Art in Glasgow, but are less often on display in western museums, making the de Young’s exhibition a rarity. articles.text: High above Napa Valley, on the rugged slopes of Pritchard Hill, Chappellet Winery occupies a place that is both physically and historically distinctive. Founded by Donn and Molly Chappellet in 1967, the family winery was one of the pioneers of Napa Valley’s modern wine era and helped establish mountain vineyards as a source of some of California’s most distinguished Cabernet Sauvignon. Donn Chappellet came to winemaking with an ambitious goal: to produce wines that could stand alongside the great First Growths of Bordeaux. After selling his interest in a successful food-service company, he and Molly moved their family to Pritchard Hill, then an isolated and largely unproven piece of Napa Valley. Following the advice of legendary winemaker André Tchelistcheff, they planted vines on the steep, rocky terrain. It was hardly an obvious choice. Pritchard Hill is considerably warmer and more rugged than much of the valley floor, with elevations at the Chappellet estate ranging from about 800 to 1,800 feet. But those difficult conditions turned out to be an advantage. The thin, well-drained soils and varied elevations and exposures naturally limit vine vigor and produce small quantities of intensely flavored grapes. Today the estate is divided into 48 vineyard blocks, each reflecting differences in soil, slope and exposure. Chappellet’s first commercial Cabernet Sauvignon appeared in 1969, establishing a tradition that remains at the heart of the winery. Although the original vineyards also included Chenin Blanc, Riesling, Chardonnay, Gamay and Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon gradually became the estate’s signature. The winery’s Pritchard Hill Cabernet Sauvignon is now its flagship wine, produced from the finest fruit on the mountain. The winery itself is almost as memorable as the wines. articles.text: A new program called Weavers is getting Piedmont seniors and teens together for social visits aiming at intergenerational connectivity. The Piedmont chapter of Weavers was tested from April to June with more than 40 participants, thanks to the help of founding members and Piedmont students Allyson Huynh and Luca Laforte. Gloria Lee of Oakland founded the program along with Kristin Richmond, the co-founder of Revolution Food. Lee, who lectures at Cal and Stanford, contacted Ken Li, the Crew Advisor of Piedmont Community Service Crew to get the program off the ground. She was then introduced to PHS juniors Huynh and Laforte, meeting in March to discuss the launch. Huynh started a Weavers’ Instagram to recruit teenagers to participate and went door to door in Piedmont to find interested seniors. Lee explained the origination of the program. “My sons Corbin and Asher really benefited from their friendship with an older neighbor, who first invited them over to bake cookies when they were four and six years old,” she said. Richmond’s son Caleb similarly started a window washing business and noticed that the older adults hiring him enjoyed chatting more than they cared about clean windows. The Piedmont program in the spring started with six weekly visits between “Weavers,” teens, and “Silvers” (seniors), and each visit lasted 60-90 minutes. “We think it’s really important that these relationships are mutually beneficial. We saw other well-meaning programs out there that treat one person in the relationship as someone who needs Olivia Tran (left), Mary Carter, Dick Carter, and Elly Mak. to be taken care of — but no one really wants to be the recipient of charity,” said Lee. Helping one another and building community is at the forefront of this work. “While Weavers are able to lend a hand to Silvers with technology support, gardening, and light organizing. I have found that people really do enjoy just talking. It makes a difference in your day just to have a good long conversation with someone,” said Huynh. In the Spring pilot of Piedmont and Oakland region, there were 23 Weavers and 23 Silvers. Piedmont’s Dick and Mary Carter signed up for the program because they like the concepts of intergeneration connection and people helping one another. They also joined because of the recommendation to join from longtime friend Ken Li. “Just meeting and talking with these delightful, energetic young people is delightful,” said Dick Carter. “I think older adults who don’t have much contact and communications with teenagers would especially benefit and enjoy the program. However, everyone can benefit from having more contact with people who are different from them.” Carter also spoke of a reaffirmation that the future is in good hands after the meetings, a comment echoed by many of the Silvers participating. “Intergenerational community to me feels like everyone, regardless of age, having positive relationships,” said Huynh. “It feels like everyone coming together and being friends, making memories, and having fun. Having this kind of community is super important because really, everyone benefits.” “Weavers will have the opportunity not only to demonstrate their skills but also have those skills validated by an older adult with lots of life experience. One of the important things about this program is that both sides contribute and both sides benefit,” said Lee. All participants of the spring pilot signed up again for the fall sessions which begins this month. Teenagers and seniors who want to learn about the program can visit beaweaver.com or call 510-788-0260. Gael Pardi (left) and Asher Breeden. Nava Shaham (left) and Olivia Bailey. Co-founder Kris Richmond leads a focus group with Silvers (seniors) in Mill Valley, the site of the program’s second pilot.

articles.text: The Ghirardelli house and other stories on Highland and Bonita Last Wednesday the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group drew 50 walkers and seven K-9 best friends to the Exedra for Part 2 of a walk they had enjoyed in early August. Mary Carter was back to lead, again drawing on her former Wildwood School Piedmont history lessons and Ann Swift’s 2007 Cottages and Castles – The Centennial Houses of the City of Piedmont for a second visit to historical, pre-1906 San Francisco Earthquake Piedmont homes. Swift’s book describes 173 of the city’s historic homes that qualified in 2007 as Piedmont Centennial Homes. August’s walk covered mostly Hillside Avenue; this one turned to Highland and Bonita. Mary started up Highland at 636, commonly known as “The Ghirardelli House,” one of the more noteworthy and beautiful homes in central Piedmont. George and Grace Howell built a Mission Style home there before 1903, then hired A.W. Smith to build a larger Tudor next door at 630 Highland on a lot they owned. In 1905 they sold 636 to Joseph and Ellen (Ellie) Ghirardelli, the son and daughter-inlaw of Domenico Ghirardelli, the Italian-trained chocolatier who emigrated from Genoa to Uruguay in 1838, came north for the Gold Rush, and founded his chocolate company where Ghirardelli Square stands today. Joseph, born in 1852, was the third of the Ghirardellis’ eight children. He worked in the family business and was in Santa Cruz when the 1906 earthquake struck. With no transportation available back to the East Bay, he set out on foot and died of a heart attack on the way. He never lived in the Highland Avenue house, which was then being remodeled from Mission Style to the Colonial Revival we see today. Ellie and their two daughters moved in once the work was finished. Back up Highland, the group passed 1900 Oakland Avenue — “The Rackliffe House,” built in 1899 with captivating witch’s cap turrets — and, across the street, the turreted Queen Anne at 225 Highland. John and Annie Hendry sold lots there to Maggie Perry in 1897; she built the house in 1898 and rented to the Hendrys, who eventually bought it from her. A 1910 proposal to line the street with retail stores set off a battle among the neighbors, and the widening that followed in 1911 claimed Annie’s front garden. She had the house put on rollers and moved with a significant setback so that her garden would never again be violated. At Highland’s corner with Moraga Avenue stands 7 Highland, built in 1907 by Frank C. Havens’ Piedmont Development Company to showcase homes and sell lots in Piedmont. Current homeowner Patty Edmonds came out to tell the walkers her family’s history with it: her mother and stepfather lived there 55 years until their passings, and Patty and her husband, Art, moved in later. She said the couple recently noticed a bulge around the front entrance and discovered the wire support for the stucco exterior had fully deteriorated after 120 years. It has been replaced, and the exterior will be painted soon to complete the project. Down Moraga and up Bonita, the walkers noted 24 Bonita, built in 1904 with deep eaves and brown shingles, and 42 Bonita, built in 1905 — a “hybrid house,” Mary said, originally wood-sided Colonial Revival until brown shingles added sometime after 1926 gave it a Craftsman look. Its owner, spotting half a hundred visitors outside, came out to see what was going on; the words “Wednesday Walkers” explained everything. He provided a little more information about the home but declined to be identified for this report. Farther along, 112 Bonita is a “twin house” to a Hillside home built in 1905. The Queen Anne “Berkenfeld House” at 227 Bonita has rooftop gargoyles, spindle work posts, corbels, and window panels. Its initial owner was one of the original Piedmont volunteer firefighters, who helped save a house at 116 Hillside — and possibly the block — during Among those participating were Moya Robinson with K-9 best friend Petunia, Albert Chen, Bill Ahern, Juliane Jacqueline, Kristin Howard, Audrey Sung, Matt Truesdell, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Rich Harms, Matt Gerhardt, Judy Love, Debbie Powell, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Cathy Laymon, Peggy Shultz, Noemi Alvarado, Vicki Trimbach, Pat Nicholas, Jim Kuo, Brian Hamlin, Denny McGee, Mary Ann Barnes, Greg Keller, Claudine Bach, Caskey Weston, Melba Yee, Chuck Oraftik, Rick Eigenbrode, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mark Davis, Sherry Jacobs, Mary Carter, Charlene Louie, Mary Henderson, Alan Jolly, Sanghi Wagner, Dan Sedonis, Deborah Curtin with K-9 best friend Brie, Pat Keller, Bern Schild, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Gwen, and Dick Carter. articles.text: Gary Laymon, 68, of Piedmont, California, passed away peacefully on July 24, 2026 after a nearly two-year journey with cancer. He was a cherished husband, father, son, brother, neighbor, colleague, and friend and he will be deeply missed. Gary was born in 1958 to Rose and Maurice Laymon in Indianapolis, Indiana. They moved to the Bay Area, where his younger sister, Nancy, was born in 1961. The young family lived between Mount Tamalpais and Mount Diablo, eventually settling in Danville. The Laymons were involved in their local church, and Gary loved going to the youth group. He also enjoyed singing in the church choir, bowling, playing golf, and doing yard work when he wasn’t pulling goofy pranks with his friends. He graduated from Monte Vista High School in 1976, and began pursuing a degree in Landscape Architecture at Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo that fall. After graduating, Gary landed a job with Guzzardo & Associates, a landscape architecture firm in San Francisco, where he would spend the next 46 years. He began attending First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley in the ’80s, meeting many dear friends and was involved in several fellowship groups. Through a young adult group, he met Cathy Ives, who invited him to a party marking the anniversary of the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake. His world was rocked as through some blessed misread signals each believed the other to be flirting, and suddenly Gary saw his friend in a new light. They were together ever since the “Great Misunderstanding,” marrying October 3rd, 1992, and welcoming Emily in 1996, Claire in 1999, and Elissa in 2002. Gary was a devoted father, known for his silliness, humor, and sense of adventure. He shared with his daughters his love of the ocean, music, gardens, art, bike riding, and travel creating countless memories along the way. As a young family, the Laymons enjoyed bike rides in wine country, hikes in the East Bay Hills, annual trips to Half Moon Bay’s pumpkin patches, Disneyland trips, summer musicals at Woodminster theaters, sports games, innumerable dance recitals, and summers with extended family at Mount Hermon, where Gary had gone as a child. As the girls grew older, the family traveled together to France, Spain, and Italy, went wine tasting and bike riding, toured an excessive number of gardens and art museums, and took thousands upon thousands of photos. In 2000, Gary became partner and owner at The Guzzardo Partnership with his long-term colleague Paul Lettieri. Gary was passionate about landscape design and loved working with clients to bring projects to life. He also enjoyed mentoring and teaching colleagues who were newer to the profession. Any drive in the car with Gary inevitably included him pointing out the many, many projects he had worked on over the years. In his free time, Gary painted with acrylics, moving through phases of vineyards, palm trees, scenes from his travels, Gary with his paintings at the Piedmont Art Walk Piedmont resident Gary Laymon died on July 24, 2026, at age 68. surfboards and abstract pieces inspired by his favorite jazz compositions. He loved sharing his art, displaying it at church and participating in the Piedmont Art Walk over several years. Gary’s faith was integral to his life. He started the day with Bible study and prayer. He saw needs and felt led to help. He was known for being kind, humble, gentle, grateful and generous. He was involved in several projects at church and led work groups at CityTeam Oakland, an organization near and dear to his heart. Mostly, Gary loved the routine of the life he loved: commuting to work in SF by bike and ferry, church on Sunday with Cathy by his side and being the last to leave the sanctuary, never having chatted with quite enough people; drinking Peet’s coffee every morning from a cup he painted when the kids were young at Color Me Mine; creating immersive scenes from scripture in his garage-turned-studio space with his paint brush; marveling at the miracle of streaming music on Spotify; calling out “sunset alert!” in the house when the view was too stunning to miss; working hard in the yard, always wanting to make things more beautiful. It was never enough to marvel at something alone. Gary wanted to share his awe, share his vision, and share the beautiful things he created to the fullest extent possible. Gary is survived by his wife, Cathy Laymon of Piedmont; his daughters, Emily West (Nick) of San Diego, Claire Laymon of Piedmont, Elissa Laymon of San Francisco; his mother, Rose Laymon, of Walnut Creek, and his sister, Nancy Laymon, of Chico. He was preceded in death by his father, Maurice Laymon. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that donations be made in Gary’s memory to CityTeam Oakland. articles.text: James Richard Saunders, Jr., known as Jim to family and friends and “Pops” to his grandchildren, passed away peacefully at his home in Piedmont, California on July 11, 2026, surrounded by family. He was 82 years old. Jim was born on August 5, 1943, in Omaha, Nebraska. He grew up in Menlo Park, California, where he attended Menlo-Atherton High School. He went on to graduate from Johns Hopkins University before earning his medical degree from the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. While at Menlo-Atherton, Jim met Lynn, who would become his wife and lifelong partner. They were married for 59 years and built a life together while raising their three children and, in later years, enjoying the company of their six grandchildren, all of whom live within a mile. Jim practiced internal medicine for more than 40 years, spending the majority of his career with Oakland Medical Group. He took great pride in the lasting relationships he built with his patients, many of whom remained with him throughout his career. Medicine was more than a profession to Jim; it was a passion he cared deeply about and approached with dedication, compassion, and integrity. Outside of medicine, Jim had a lifelong love of the outdoors and stayed active through running, cycling, and hiking. He was a devoted Oakland sports fan and always knew the latest scores. Whether following the A’s, RaidJames Richard Saunders passed away peacefully on July 11, 2026. He was 82 years old. ers, or Warriors, he enjoyed keeping up with his teams through every season. Jim was also well known for his quick wit and sense of humor. Jim is survived by his devoted wife, Lynn; his son, Vince Saunders and his wife, Michelle, and their children, Henry and Charlie; his son, Jamie Saunders and his wife, Teebie, and their children, George and Jane; and his daughter, Ashley Stevanovic and her husband, Andreja, and their children, Luka and Nicholas. He was preceded in death by his parents, James and Marion Saunders, and his sister, Joanne. Jim will be remembered as a dedicated physician, a loyal friend, and a devoted husband, father, and grandfather. His family will miss his humor, his steady presence, and the many ways he quietly showed his love over the years. In lieu of flowers, the family kindly requests that donations be made to the charity of your choice in Jim’s memory.

Something has happened, but he is just fine and everyone has been told to remain in place. Message two has an edge of uncertainty to it, yet remains reassuring. There are six calls in all, each seeming more fraught than the previous one, until the last message (“hello…are you there? Are you there?”) abruptly stops, followed by a long moment of silence. Oskar, who has turned on the television, watches in disbelief as the towers fall, as if in slow motion, each vanishing into billowing clouds of dust. Horrified, he runs to his room and crawls under his bed, waiting for his mother, Linda (Sandra Bullock), to return from work. Finally she arrives, and knowing what has occurred coaxes him out and into her arms. Oskar is incapable of accepting the loss of his father, his grief immeasurable, and when his mother has an empty-casket funeral, he refuses to attend, observing the ceremony from a distance, his denial palpable. And so a year passes, and finally, reluctantly, Oskar enters his father’s den and begins to look through his things. And when taking down a box, he knocks a blue vase off the shelf, breaking it. Among the fragments he discovers a small envelope with the name “Black” written on it. Inside he finds an unusual, corrugated key. Oskar holds the key in his hand, and it is in that moment that he becomes convinced that the key fits a lock, a box perhaps, that contains a message from his father. And thus we learn, through flashbacks, that over the years Thomas has created what he called “reconnaissance expeditions,” a scavenger hunt of sorts, which sends Oskar out into the streets of New York in search of what they call “the sixth borough.” And so attaching the key to a lanyard, which he wears around his neck, Oskar is inspired to begin a similar expedition. He starts by looking through a massive NYC phone book, and finds that there are 472 Blacks listed. His mission, kept a secret from his mother, is to visit all of them, asking if they recognize the key. His first stop is at the home of Abby Black (Viola Davis), and it’s during his conversation with her that he mentions he has been tested for Asperger’s Syndrome with inconclusive results. We know that Oskar is precocious, at times brusque, highly verbal, but we soon learn that Thomas’ expeditions were about much more than simply a sixth borough hunt, but a way of sending his son into a world in which he is inherently uncomfortable. Abby has no idea about the key, and so Oskar continues, from Black to Black, showing each of them the key, and using his father’s vintage camera takes their photograph, which he keeps in a notebook. To refer to Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close as a work of art may verge on hyperbole. And yet, doesn’t it represent the use of images and narrative as only film can, to explore the depths of grief and loss while focusing on the emotions of a young boy who struggles to find meaning in what he angrily judges is meaningless. The key becomes a metaphor for Oskar’s arduous and at times fraught search for answers to questions that are timeless: to what purpose? To what end? And, ultimately, why? They will continue to lead the classroom in its new home, bringing continuity and stability to the transition. The new location offers a light-filled, calm and inviting setting for the school’s play-based approach to early childhood learning. PPS remains the only licensed preschool of its kind in the area built around social-emotional learning as a core part of its curriculum. A day at Piedmont Play School Each day at PPS blends structured and child-led play, giving children space to explore, build friendships, and develop independence alongside caring, familiar teachers. PPS’s play-based, mixedage curriculum is intentionally designed to strengthen the social and emotional skills that matter most as children grow. Mixedage classes encourage younger children to learn from older peers and give older children opportunities to lead and mentor — building confidence, empathy, and communication skills. Educators increasingly point to strong social-emotional foundations as a key predictor of success when children enter TK and Kindergarten, where academic and behavioral expectations have never been higher. PPS’s approach is designed to help prepare children for that transition both academically and emotionally. Teacher Michelle Ritchie has been with Piedmont Play School since 2013. A Co-Op model built for busy families PPS operates as a light co-op by design. Families are asked to contribute in small, manageable ways rather than large time commitments, making it possible for working parents to still be present and engaged in their child’s classroom experience. Many parents describe their volunteer hours as some of the most rewarding time they spend with their kids. For PPS President & CEO June Groboske, the co-op model is about more than the preschool. It’s the starting point for a much longer relationship between families and their community. “Our co-op model is where a lifelong connection to our school community begins,” said Groboske. “PPS parents discover early on what meaningful school involvement looks like. Working side by side with teachers and other parents gives families a firsthand appreciation for the school, classroom, and community dynamics, helping parents learn how to best support teachers and students alike. That strong foundation naturally carries forward — so many of our PPS parents go on to serve as parent board officers, school committee chairs, and active community leaders throughout PUSD.” With this move to Clarewood Drive, PPS parents, alumni, and teachers preserved a philosophy of early childhood education, a group of beloved teachers, and a place where families can be genuinely involved in their children’s earliest school experiences. The comfort in knowing the school will carry on, paired with genuine enthusiasm for what’s ahead, has echoed throughout the PPS community as the school settles into its new space. To learn more about PPS, please visit piedmontplayschool. org. Follow along: @piedmontplayschoolca on Instagram. articles.text: As fall begins, the Piedmont Fire Department urges residents to set aside time to complete a simple, easy-to-follow at-home wildfire evacuation exercise with their household. The exercise provides step-by-step instructions and discussion prompts in a short video that families, housemates, and neighbors can use to transform their wildfire “what ifs” into a tangible, actionable plan. The short exercise helps you spot gaps, talk through decisions, and walk away more confident about what to do if a wildfire comes. What to expect: • A realistic, local wildfire scenario based on conditions in Piedmont • Simple, pause-and-discuss prompts for each stage of • • • evacuation A downloadable worksheet to capture your household’s plan and next steps A calm, supportive narrator to walk you through the process Total time: 30-45 minutes Watch the video and download the worksheet at piedmont.ca.gov/ WildfirePlan. Find additional wildfire preparedness resources at piedmont.ca.gov/Wildfire. The at-home evacuation exercise is one part of the Piedmont Fire Department’s broader work partnering with community members to build a safer, more resilient Piedmont. Last year, the department conducted a practical evacuation drill for the Blair/ Scenic/Alta neighborhood, giving them a hands-on opportunity to test their own evacuation plans. Firefighters also provide year-round public education, coordinate training with regional partners, and offer home visits to help residents understand steps they can take to harden their properties. The department also recently led the development of Piedmont’s Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, engaging residents in a collaborative process to create a 5-year roadmap that identifies steps the city can take to reduce the effects of disasters before they happen. Each household that completes the at-home exercise adds another layer of readiness to these efforts – strengthening not just their own plans, but our community’s resilience as a whole.
